title: Did the win-back email actually lift retention?

scenario.role: You're the data analyst at Lumen
scenario.situation: In Q3, Marketing sent a "win-back" email to a slice of the user base. Dana, the VP of Marketing, pulled the retention numbers and is thrilled: users who received the email retained at about 55% over the next 90 days, versus about 23% for everyone else — a 32-point gap. She wants to pour the entire Q4 budget into scaling the campaign to the whole base, and she needs your sign-off on the analysis first.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "The win-back email lifts 90-day retention by ~30 points. Scaling it to everyone is the highest-ROI move we have."
scenario.question: Is the lift real? Estimate the campaign's actual effect on 90-day retention, and tell Dana whether — and how — to scale it.

columns.name: signup_month
columns.description: Month the user first subscribed (YYYY-MM), trailing 12 months

columns.name: plan_tier
columns.description: Subscription tier: basic, plus, or premium

columns.name: region
columns.description: User region: NA, EU, or APAC

columns.name: engagement_score
columns.description: Pre-campaign engagement (0-100), measured BEFORE the win-back email went out

columns.name: got_campaign
columns.description: 1 if the user received the Q3 win-back email, else 0

columns.name: retained_90d
columns.description: 1 if the user was still subscribed 90 days later, else 0

guidingQuestions: What's the naive 90-day retention gap between users who got the campaign and those who didn't? (This is the number Dana is quoting.)
Who actually received the campaign? Compare the two groups on engagement_score — the score measured BEFORE the email went out.
Which variable confounds the comparison, and why does it inflate the naive gap?
Estimate the campaign's effect after accounting for that confounder — e.g. stratify on engagement (deciles) or model retained_90d ~ engagement + got_campaign. How big is the honest effect now?
What do you tell Dana? Should she scale the campaign to the whole base, and does the data support her ROI claim?
suggestedApproach: Reproduce the stakeholder's number first — compute 90-day retention for got_campaign = 1 vs 0 — so you know exactly what claim you're testing.
Don't credit the email yet. Describe who received it: compare the campaigned and non-campaigned groups across the other columns before attributing the gap to the campaign.
If the groups already differ on something that also drives retention, that variable is confounding the comparison — decide how to account for it (stratify, match, or model).
Re-estimate the effect holding that variable constant, and check the answer is stable across at least two methods.
Turn the adjusted number into a recommendation — and note what Dana would need (e.g. a randomised holdout) to trust it next time.

notebook.intro: Five steps: reproduce the retention gap, describe who actually got the email, then re-estimate the effect on comparable users.

cells.title: Reproduce the headline
cells.explain: Compute 90-day retention for the campaigned and non-campaigned groups, so the exact claim is on the table.
cells.code:
rates = df.groupby("got_campaign")["retained_90d"].mean() * 100
headline = rates[1] - rates[0]
print(f"headline gap (campaigned - not): {headline:+.2f} pts")
rates.round(2)
cells.reads: The gap is large. Nothing so far says the email caused it.

cells.title: Describe who received it
cells.explain: Before crediting the campaign, compare the two groups on everything else you have. A targeted send will show up here.
cells.code:
profile = df.groupby("got_campaign")[["engagement_score"]].mean()
profile["n"] = df.groupby("got_campaign").size()
print("who got the email:")
print(profile.round(2))
pd.crosstab(df["got_campaign"], df["plan_tier"], normalize="index").round(3) * 100
cells.reads: The campaigned group was already far more engaged before the email went out. The groups were never comparable.

cells.title: Check the confounder drives the outcome
cells.explain: A variable only confounds if it also predicts retention. Bin engagement and look at retention across the bins.
cells.code:
df["engagement_band"] = pd.qcut(df["engagement_score"], 10, labels=False, duplicates="drop")
by_band = df.groupby("engagement_band")["retained_90d"].mean() * 100
print("retention by engagement decile (%)")
by_band.round(1)
cells.reads: Engagement predicts retention strongly on its own — which is exactly what makes the raw comparison unusable.

cells.title: Hold engagement constant
cells.explain: Compare campaigned against non-campaigned inside each engagement decile, then re-weight to one common mix.
cells.code:
within = df.groupby(["engagement_band", "got_campaign"])["retained_90d"].mean().unstack()
weights = df["engagement_band"].value_counts(normalize=True)
adjusted = within.mul(weights, axis=0).sum() * 100
adj_effect = adjusted[1] - adjusted[0]
print(f"adjusted effect: {adj_effect:+.2f} pts")
within.round(3)
cells.reads: Within like-for-like users the effect is a small fraction of the headline.

cells.title: Put the two numbers side by side
cells.explain: The number that would be quoted, against the number that survives adjustment.
cells.code:
pd.DataFrame(
    {"effect (pts)": [headline, adj_effect]},
    index=["raw comparison", "same engagement level"],
).round(2)
cells.reads: Most of the headline was selection — who was chosen to receive the email, not what the email did.

teachingNote.naiveRead: Campaigned users retained at ~55% vs ~23% for the rest — a +31.7 point gap. Taken at face value, the win-back email looks like the single highest-leverage retention tool Lumen has, and scaling it to everyone looks like free money.
teachingNote.theTrap: The campaign was NOT randomly assigned. It was sent preferentially to users who were already engaged: campaigned users average an engagement_score of 59, versus 36 for everyone else. Engagement is also the strongest driver of retention. So the two groups were already very different before a single email went out — most of that 32-point gap is the pre-existing engagement difference, not the email. This is textbook selection bias: comparing treated vs untreated when the treated were hand-picked to be better.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Once you hold engagement constant — stratify users into engagement deciles and average the within-decile campaign effect, or run retained_90d ~ engagement_score + got_campaign — the campaign's effect collapses to about +1.9 points. Real, but roughly a tenth of the headline number. The email nudges retention slightly; it does not lift it 30 points.
howToGetThere: Compute the raw retention gap: mean(retained_90d) for got_campaign=1 minus got_campaign=0. You'll get ~+31.7 pts — Dana's number.
Before attributing it to the email, profile who was treated: group by got_campaign and look at mean engagement_score. The campaigned group is far more engaged (≈59 vs ≈36).
Recognise engagement_score as a confounder: it drives BOTH who got the campaign and who retains, so it inflates the naive comparison.
Adjust for it — stratify on engagement deciles and take the size-weighted within-stratum difference, or fit a logistic/linear model with engagement as a covariate. Any valid method lands near +2 pts.
Sense-check: the adjusted effect should be far smaller than the naive one, and stable across methods.
teachingNote.lesson: When a treatment isn't randomly assigned, a raw difference between the treated and untreated is a confounded comparison, not a causal effect. Before you attribute an outcome to an intervention, ask: who received it, and were they already different? Here the win-back email was sent to the users most likely to stay anyway. Adjust for the pre-existing difference and the real effect is a fraction of the headline. Scaling the campaign to the whole base will not reproduce a 30-point lift — budget against the ~2-point honest effect, and if you want a trustworthy number, run a randomised holdout next time.
